profiles.meeting_scenario: Baylor University is planning a brainstorming meeting to shape the next iteration of its six-week International Technology Entrepreneurship (I5) summer program in Shanghai, where U.S. engineering/computer science and business students work with Chinese students and company partners on innovation projects. The immediate context is that the program leaders want a refreshed concept note for internal approval and partner outreach, drawing on lessons from prior Europe trips while adapting to Shanghai's faster-paced startup and multinational ecosystem. The agenda is to generate and loosely screen candidate program features for the Shanghai version: what kinds of company collaborations to include, how to structure interdisciplinary teams, what 'immersion' should look like, and how to package cultural training alongside project work. The expected outcome is a shortlist of 3-4 promising program design ideas that both participants believe are ready to fold into the concept note and discuss with external partners.

members.name: Dr. Emily Harper
members.role: Associate Dean for Global Programs, School of Engineering and Computer Science
members.expertise: engineering education, study abroad program design, faculty-led international experiential learning
members.background: Emily has helped build Baylor's ECS study abroad offerings over the last six years and was involved in multiple Europe-based program iterations; she is experienced in aligning overseas experiences with accreditation expectations and academic credit structures.
members.private_state: She wants the Shanghai program to feel genuinely distinctive from the Europe trips while remaining administratively manageable, academically defensible for engineering faculty, and low-risk enough to secure internal approval without triggering a long compliance review.
hidden_assumptions: When a study abroad program is described as 'immersive,' it still has a faculty-scaffolded rhythm with structured reflection, guided site visits, and supervised team work rather than open-ended local integration.

A 'real-world company project' in an academic summer program usually means a bounded exploratory challenge suitable for student learning, not a client-style deliverable that a company expects to implement immediately.

If a feature is said to work 'with Chinese students,' the natural unit is a few pre-arranged mixed teams anchored through a partner university course or organized cohort, not ad hoc collaboration across a wider local startup scene.
Reusing the Europe playbook is acceptable as long as the visible setting, company examples, and cultural modules are localized for China.

members.name: Jason Liu
members.role: Director of Corporate Partnerships, Hankamer School of Business
members.expertise: entrepreneurship programming, industry engagement, cross-border innovation partnerships
members.background: Jason has spent several years building relationships with multinational firms and startup incubators in Asia and joined the I5 effort when the business school integrated commercialization into the previously engineering-focused abroad model.
members.private_state: He wants the Shanghai version to look market-facing and globally connected enough to attract strong company partners, donor interest, and high-achieving students, while signaling that the business school is bringing something more ambitious than a lightly modified engineering study trip.
hidden_assumptions: When a program is called 'immersive,' students should spend substantial time embedded in live entrepreneurial environments such as incubators, company offices, and founder meetings, with less classroom mediation than a traditional faculty-led trip.

A 'real-world company project' should produce something a partner could plausibly use soon after the program, even if modest, because companies engage more seriously when there is visible near-term value.

Working 'with Chinese students' naturally includes leveraging startup club networks, incubator affiliates, and student founders in Shanghai, not only a formal classroom cohort from one partner university.

Lessons from the Europe trips mainly establish credibility; the Shanghai redesign should depart materially in structure because China-based innovation partners will expect a more fast-moving, externally engaged format.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as an 'immersive' Shanghai experience
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both repeatedly endorse making the program 'more immersive.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means deeper cultural and interdisciplinary learning through structured, faculty-guided exposure, reflection sessions, and a carefully curated weekly schedule.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means students spending more time inside live startup and corporate environments with looser academic scaffolding and more field-based interaction.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see 'immersion' as obviously desirable and contextually self-explanatory for study abroad, so the shared positive term creates false consensus without inviting operational clarification.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that U.S. students should work 'with Chinese students' throughout the six weeks.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means a designated cohort from one partner university in Shanghai who join mixed teams for scheduled project sessions and selected cultural activities.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes a broader network of local participants such as incubator-affiliated student founders, club members, and graduate entrepreneurs who can rotate through teams, events, and mentoring touchpoints.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds concrete enough to both participants because each already pictures a plausible Shanghai student ecosystem, and neither expects the other to mean a materially different boundary around who is included.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both want every team to tackle a 'real-world company project.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks a project is real-world if it is sourced from an actual company and gives students authentic problem context, even if the output is a concept exploration, opportunity map, or prototype recommendation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks a project is real-world only if the company can realistically act on the student output soon, such as using a market entry brief, customer validation summary, or pilot-ready demo direction.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They agree on the legitimacy marker of involving actual companies, so the deeper difference in evidentiary standard for 'real-world' remains hidden under a term that sounds specific and shared.

misalignment_points.topic: Using the 'Europe model' as a starting point
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'build from what worked in Europe.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes this means retaining the Europe program's core academic architecture and simply adapting examples, partners, and cultural modules to Shanghai.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes the Europe experience only provides rough lessons and credibility, while the Shanghai version should be structurally reworked to fit China's innovation tempo and external partnership expectations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both positively reference prior success, the phrase functions as reassuring continuity; neither notices that one is invoking a template and the other is invoking a springboard.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to feel fresh enough that nobody says we're just transplanting the Europe trip, but I also need a concept note that still rests on a familiar academic structure. If we build from what worked in Europe, we can preserve the credit logic, faculty oversight, and assessment pieces and simply localize the companies, case examples, and cultural programming for Shanghai. That should keep internal approval smoother and avoid a sprawling compliance conversation.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time, Jason. My hope today is that we can sketch a refreshed Shanghai concept for I5 that builds from what worked in Europe but still feels distinctive enough for the next cycle. If we leave with three or four design ideas we both feel good about, we can turn that into a solid concept note pretty quickly.

turns.inner_thought: This is the moment to push the Shanghai version into something much more externally engaged than the Europe trips. For me, building from what worked in Europe mostly means using prior success as proof of concept, not carrying over the same structure. If we can make this more immersive and centered on real-world company activity, it will be far more compelling to firms, donors, and top students.
turns.utterance: Absolutely. To me, Shanghai is the right place to make the program more immersive and more visibly tied to real-world company activity than some of the earlier versions. That would give it a clearer identity and make the story stronger for both students and partners.

turns.inner_thought: A six-week rhythm needs to be coherent and supervised: cultural modules, company visits, team work blocks, and regular faculty touchpoints. Working with Chinese students should mean a reliable partner-university cohort we can schedule around, not a diffuse set of people drifting in and out. That will make the experience immersive in a way that is academically legible and manageable.
turns.utterance: One possible frame is a six-week arc with guided cultural modules, scheduled company visits, and mixed engineering-business teams working with Chinese students on innovation challenges. That would let us connect the academic side and the market side without losing the overall shape of the program.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and I'd like those teams spending real time inside incubators and startup offices, not just visiting them. When I hear working with Chinese students, I picture tapping into startup clubs, student founders, and incubator-affiliated young entrepreneurs who are already close to active ventures. That ecosystem access is what could make Shanghai stand apart.
turns.utterance: I like that. Building on it, I think we should give teams regular time in incubators and startup offices so they're working with Chinese students who are already close to live ventures. That would reinforce the Shanghai angle in a really natural way.

turns.inner_thought: The company element needs to be authentic but bounded. If each team has a project sourced from a real firm, students can engage a genuine problem context while still producing something suitable for a summer academic program. Multinationals and Chinese firms would both work, as long as the challenge can anchor technical and business learning rather than becoming an uncontrolled client engagement.
turns.utterance: Yes, and I think the company piece will be strongest if each team has a real-world company project from a multinational or Chinese firm that can anchor both technical and business learning. That gives everyone something concrete to work around from the start.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—partners will engage seriously only if the output looks useful soon after the program ends. A real-world company project should end with something a company could plausibly pick up and use, especially around commercialization, customer discovery, or market entry. I don't need to say all that now; Emily is clearly on board with making the company work meaningful.
turns.utterance: Agreed. I also think partners will be much more excited if students can hand back something usable at the end, especially on market-facing or commercialization questions. That makes the real-world company project feel meaningful on both sides.

turns.inner_thought: To keep this approval-ready, we need the familiar Europe rhythm underneath: weekly reflection, faculty checkpoints, and a steady cadence that documents learning. For me, that is exactly how an immersive program stays coherent and credit-friendly. We can update the content for Shanghai without abandoning the structure that has worked before.
turns.utterance: One thing I'd want to preserve as we build from what worked in Europe is a weekly rhythm with reflection sessions and faculty checkpoints, so the immersive piece stays academically coherent and credit-friendly. We can still make it feel dynamic while giving it a clear backbone.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with some structure, but I do not want the Europe format to become the template. In Shanghai, partner schedules will move quickly, and founder access often comes together on short notice. Building from what worked in Europe should mean keeping the credibility while opening the calendar enough for more fluid, field-based engagement.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I do think the Europe experience gives us a strong base, but in Shanghai the schedule should leave room for fast-moving partner interactions and founder-led sessions outside a fixed classroom cadence. That flexibility may be part of what makes it genuinely immersive there.

turns.inner_thought: A stable cohort model will help enormously. If we pair Baylor students with a partner-university group in Shanghai and keep those mixed teams together, faculty can monitor collaboration, and students can build continuity over six weeks. That's what I mean by working with Chinese students throughout the program.
turns.utterance: Another design idea is to pair Baylor students with a partner-university cohort in Shanghai and have those mixed teams stay together across the six weeks. If they're working with Chinese students throughout, that continuity could really strengthen the experience.

turns.inner_thought: Great starting point, but I want the circle to be wider than one university cohort. We should also draw in entrepreneurship clubs, incubator networks, and student founders who can appear at key moments and expand the network effect. In my mind that's still simply working with Chinese students throughout—just in a richer Shanghai ecosystem.
turns.utterance: I really like that, and I think we can extend it by including a wider circle of Chinese students who could join project milestones and mentoring sessions over the six weeks. That keeps the teams working with Chinese students throughout while also opening up more of the local ecosystem.

turns.inner_thought: For the end of program, we need visible evidence of learning that faculty and internal reviewers will recognize: company insights, prototype directions, and cultural reflection. That is a strong way to demonstrate a real-world company project and an immersive experience without promising implementation outcomes we can't control.
turns.utterance: For a capstone, I could see a final showcase where teams present company insights, prototype directions, and cultural takeaways as evidence of a successful real-world immersion. That would give us something concrete for assessment and for storytelling.

turns.inner_thought: This is sounding promising. I hear alignment on an immersive Shanghai model, real-world company projects, and building from what worked in Europe while making the partner side much more visible. I'll draft the outreach in a way that foregrounds company engagement and market relevance; that should help us test interest quickly.
turns.utterance: I think we're pretty aligned: an immersive Shanghai model, teams working with Chinese students, real-world company projects, and a design that builds from what worked in Europe while being more tuned to company engagement. I'm happy to draft a few partner-facing idea summaries from this and circulate them for your edits.
